name: Sortition
summary: Sortition is the selection of decision-makers by random draw from the citizen body instead of by election. Its advocates hold that lots give every citizen an equal chance of holding political power, produce bodies that mirror the public, and escape campaign money, party machines and elite capture. Proposals range from replacing every elected legislator (lottocracy), through a lot-chosen chamber beside an elected one, to lot-chosen juries that only oversee officials.

scope: The modern movement for choosing political decision-makers by lot, as the scholarship names it: lottocracy (Guerrero, as set out in Jakobi's dissertation), bicameral legislature by lot (Gastil and Wright), sortition as anti-corruption oversight (Bagg), and the citizens' assemblies whose members are drawn by lot (Gasiorowska). Ancient Athenian practice is a historical precedent covered by Athenian democracy, and the wider deliberative-democracy tradition is a separate subject; neither answers here. Sortition is a method for selecting rulers, so the defining sources take positions mainly on democratic institutions, and most statements stay null.

notes: Built from five saved sources: Gastil and Wright's essay, Jakobi's dissertation on Guerrero's lottocracy, Bagg's AJPS article, Gasiorowska's study of citizens' assemblies, and Wikipedia as a finding aid. Sortition is a method of selecting officeholders, so its sources answer only on selection, representation, equality of access, parties, elite capture and the franchise; every economic, cultural, ecological, technological and foreign-policy statement is null. Themes searched: elections and parties, expertise versus ordinary citizens, bicameralism, term of office and recall, campaign money and lobbying, the franchise, constitution drafting (only Wikipedia mentions it), referendums and direct democracy, local government, minority and indigenous representation, and Gastil and Wright's Marxist postscript (Wright states there that the case for sortition fits progressive and conservative views alike, so its economics is not the ideology's). Advocates split on whether lots replace elections, so those answers are 0 at low confidence. Guerrero's original paper could not be opened (see notFound). Failing the uncertainty rule is the honest result.
